SECTION: Most Americans Support Tough Stance Toward China on Human Rights, Economic Issues - How we did this (Pages 3-4)

TOPICS: survey methodology, American public opinion on China, U.S.-China relationship, human rights, economic competition, Chinese students, survey data, weighting, open-ended responses, comparative trends

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- Pew Research Center conducted a study on American views toward China (Page 3)
- The survey included 2,596 U.S. adults from February 1 to 7, 2021 (Page 3)
- Participants were members of the American Trends Panel (ATP), an online survey panel recruited via random sampling of residential addresses (Page 3)
- The survey data is weighted to be representative of the U.S. adult population by gender, race, ethnicity, partisan affiliation, education, and other categories (Page 3)
- An open-ended question was asked, and 2,010 responses were hand-coded using a researcher-developed codebook (Page 3)
- The report references "What different survey modes and question types can tell us about Americans' views of China" and "In their own words: What Americans think about China" (Page 3)
- 89% of U.S. adults view China as a competitor or enemy (Page 4)
- 70% of respondents say the U.S. should try to promote human rights in China (Page 4)
- 55% support limiting Chinese students studying in the U.S. (Page 4)
- 53% believe it is more important to get tougher with China on economic issues than to build a strong relationship (Page 4)
- 48% think limiting China's power and influence should be a top foreign policy priority, up from 32% in 2018 (Page 4)
- 67% of Americans have "cold" feelings toward China, rating it less than 50 on a 0-100 scale (Page 4)
- The survey was conducted February 1–7, 2021 (Page 4)

SECTION: Most Americans Support Tough Stance Toward China on Human Rights, Economic Issues - Introduction (Pages 4-10)

TOPICS: American public opinion on China, U.S.-China relations, human rights concerns, economic competition, partisan divides, confidence in leaders, feeling thermometer ratings

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- 89% of U.S. adults view China as a competitor or enemy (Page 4)
- 70% support promoting human rights in China (Page 4)
- 55% support limiting Chinese students studying in the U.S. (Page 4)
- 53% believe it is more important to get tougher with China economically than to build a strong relationship (Page 4)
- 48% think limiting China's power and influence should be a top foreign policy priority (up from 32% in 2018) (Page 4)
- 67% of Americans have "cold" feelings toward China, rating it less than 50 on a 0-100 scale (Page 4)
- The share of Americans with "very cold" feelings toward China (0-24 on the scale) has doubled from 23% in 2018 to 47% in 2021 (Page 5)
- Half of Americans now say China's policy on human rights is a very serious problem for the U.S., up 7 percentage points since last year (Page 5)
- Nine-in-ten Americans say China does not respect the personal freedoms of its people (Page 5)
- One-in-five Americans (20%) mention human rights concerns when thinking about China (Page 6)
- 3% of respondents specifically focused on Uyghurs in Xinjiang (Page 6)
- Around two-thirds (64%) of Americans describe economic relations with China as somewhat or very bad (Page 7)
- 79% of Americans believe China is doing a bad job dealing with global climate change (Page 7)
- A quote from a 54-year-old man describes China as a "Leader in technology. Makes a lot of cheap products. A possible threat." (Page 7)
- 54% of Americans think China is doing a bad job dealing with the coronavirus pandemic, compared to 43% who think it's doing a good job (Page 8)
- 58% of Americans say the U.S. is doing a bad job handling the pandemic (Page 8)
- Only 15% of Americans have confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping to do the right thing in world affairs (Page 8)
- 60% of Americans have confidence in President Joe Biden to do the right thing in world affairs generally (Page 8)
- Confidence in Biden to deal effectively with China is 53%, which is lower than his confidence rating for other foreign policy issues (Page 8)
- 83% of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents have confidence in Biden to deal with China, compared to 19% of Republicans and Republican leaners (Page 8)
- Republicans are 24 percentage points more likely than Democrats to see the loss of U.S. jobs to China as a very serious problem (Page 9)
- The gap on the U.S. trade deficit with China is 19 percentage points (Page 9)
- The partisan divide on economic issues has grown over the past year (Page 9)
- Democrats and Republicans largely agree on human rights issues, including support for promoting human rights in China (Page 9)
- 67% of Americans today feel “cold” toward China (rating 0-49), up from 46% in 2018 (Page 10)
- 47% of Americans feel “very cold” toward China (rating below 25), up from 23% in 2018 (Page 10)
- The share of Americans giving China a rating of zero has nearly tripled, from 9% in 2018 to 24% in 2021 (Page 10)

SECTION: Most Americans Support Tough Stance Toward China on Human Rights, Economic Issues - Introduction (Pages 4-10)

TOPICS: American public opinion on China, U.S.-China relations, human rights concerns, economic competition, partisan divides, confidence in leaders, feeling thermometer ratings

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- 89% of U.S. adults view China as a competitor or enemy (Page 4)
- 70% support promoting human rights in China (Page 4)
- 55% support limiting Chinese students studying in the U.S. (Page 4)
- 53% believe it is more important to get tougher with China economically than to build a strong relationship (Page 4)
- 48% think limiting China's power and influence should be a top foreign policy priority (up from 32% in 2018) (Page 4)
- 67% of Americans have "cold" feelings toward China, rating it less than 50 on a 0-100 scale (Page 4)
- The share of Americans with "very cold" feelings toward China (0-24 on the scale) has doubled from 23% in 2018 to 47% in 2021 (Page 5)
- Half of Americans now say China's policy on human rights is a very serious problem for the U.S., up 7 percentage points since last year (Page 5)
- Nine-in-ten Americans say China does not respect the personal freedoms of its people (Page 5)
- One-in-five Americans (20%) mention human rights concerns when thinking about China (Page 6)
- 3% of respondents specifically focused on Uyghurs in Xinjiang (Page 6)
- Around two-thirds (64%) of Americans describe economic relations with China as somewhat or very bad (Page 7)
- 79% of Americans believe China is doing a bad job dealing with global climate change (Page 7)
- A quote from a 54-year-old man describes China as a "Leader in technology. Makes a lot of cheap products. A possible threat." (Page 7)
- 54% of Americans think China is doing a bad job dealing with the coronavirus pandemic, compared to 43% who think it's doing a good job (Page 8)
- 58% of Americans say the U.S. is doing a bad job handling the pandemic (Page 8)
- Only 15% of Americans have confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping to do the right thing in world affairs (Page 8)
- 60% of Americans have confidence in President Joe Biden to do the right thing in world affairs generally (Page 8)
- Confidence in Biden to deal effectively with China is 53%, which is lower than his confidence rating for other foreign policy issues (Page 8)
- 83% of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents have confidence in Biden to deal with China, compared to 19% of Republicans and Republican leaners (Page 8)
- Republicans are 24 percentage points more likely than Democrats to see the loss of U.S. jobs to China as a very serious problem (Page 9)
- The gap on the U.S. trade deficit with China is 19 percentage points (Page 9)
- The partisan divide on economic issues has grown over the past year (Page 9)
- Democrats and Republicans largely agree on human rights issues, including support for promoting human rights in China (Page 9)
- 67% of Americans today feel “cold” toward China (rating 0-49), up from 46% in 2018 (Page 10)
- 47% of Americans feel “very cold” toward China (rating below 25), up from 23% in 2018 (Page 10)
- The share of Americans giving China a rating of zero has nearly tripled, from 9% in 2018 to 24% in 2021 (Page 10)

VISUAL_EVIDENCE:
Tables:
- Table 1 (Page 4): Majority supports a more assertive stance on bilateral relations with China across a range of issues - Three bar charts showing percentages for different policy stances: 26% prioritize strengthening economic relations while 70% want to promote human rights; 43% oppose and 55% support limiting Chinese students; 44% prefer building a strong relationship and 53% prefer getting tougher on economic issues.
- Table: What's the first thing you think about when you think about China? (%) [OPEN-END] (Page 6): Horizontal bar chart listing categories of responses to an open-ended question, with percentages: Human rights (20%), Economy (19%), Political system (17%), Threats (13%), U.S.-China relationship (12%), Generally negative adjectives (12%), COVID-19 (7%), Population size (5%).
- Table: Confidence in President Joe Biden to handle various foreign policy issues (Page 8): Bar chart comparing confidence vs. no confidence in Biden for five tasks: Deal effectively with China (53% confidence, 46% no confidence); Improve relationships with allies (67% confidence, 32% no confidence); Deal effectively with terrorism (60% confidence, 39% no confidence); Address climate change (60% confidence, 39% no confidence); Promote democracy abroad (60% confidence, 39% no confidence).
- Table: Large partisan divides on many China-related issues – but not in concerns about human rights (Page 9): Horizontal bar chart showing percentages of Democrats/Lean Dem and Republicans/Lean Rep holding views on China, with R-D Diff: 37% vs. 72% on prioritizing toughness over building a strong relationship; 20% vs. 53% on viewing China as an enemy; 42% vs. 69% on supporting limiting Chinese students; 38% vs. 62% on having "very cold" feelings toward China; 69% vs. 72% on promoting human rights; 49% vs. 54% on seeing China's human rights policies as a very serious problem.
- Table: Distribution of Feeling Thermometer Ratings for China (Page 10): Stacked bar chart showing the percentage of U.S. adults who rated China as "Very warm," "Somewhat warm," "Neutral," "Somewhat cold," or "Very cold" in 2018 and 2021, split by Total, Rep/Lean Rep, and Dem/Lean Dem.

Figures:

This page from a Pew Research Center report presents findings on partisan divides in U.S. public opinion regarding China. It highlights significant differences between Republicans and Democrats on economic issues like job loss and trade deficits, with Republicans being much more likely to view these as serious problems. The data shows that the gap has widened over the past year. In contrast, there is broad agreement between the parties on human rights-related issues, such as supporting the promotion of human rights in China. The main visual element is a horizontal bar chart illustrating these partisan differences across several key attitudes.

**Text Evidence:**
- Republicans are 24 percentage points more likely than Democrats to see the loss of U.S. jobs to China as a very serious problem.
- The gap on the U.S. trade deficit with China is 19 percentage points.
- The partisan divide on economic issues has grown over the past year.
- Democrats and Republicans largely agree on human rights issues, including support for promoting human rights in China.
- The survey was conducted online from February 1-7, 2021, among 2,596 adults.

sections.summary:
SECTION: Most Americans Support Tough Stance Toward China on Human Rights, Economic Issues - Growing share of Americans express cold feelings toward China (Pages 10-14)

TOPICS: American public opinion on China, negative sentiment trends, partisan divides, survey methodology, demographic differences, U.S.-China relationship perceptions

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- 67% of Americans today feel “cold” toward China (rating 0-49), up from 46% in 2018 (Page 10)
- 47% of Americans feel “very cold” toward China (rating below 25), up from 23% in 2018 (Page 10)
- The share of Americans giving China a rating of zero has nearly tripled, from 9% in 2018 to 24% in 2021 (Page 10)
- Only 7% of Americans have "warm" feelings (51-75) toward China and 4% have "very warm" feelings (76-100) (Page 11)
- One-in-five Americans (20%) have neutral feelings, rating China at exactly 50 (Page 11)
- 62% of Republicans feel "very cold" (0-24) toward China, up 31 points since 2018 (Page 11)
- 38% of Democrats report "very cold" feelings, up 21 points since 2018 (Page 11)
- There has been a 26-point increase in negative views since 2018 (Page 11)
- 66% of those surveyed by phone had an unfavorable view of China, compared with 79% of those surveyed online (Page 12)
- The feeling thermometer uses a 0-100 scale where 51+ is "warm," 50 is neutral, and below 50 is "cold" (Page 12)
- The percentage of people who say they are "cold" toward China increased from 46% in 2018 to 67% in 2021, a 21 percentage point increase (Page 12)
- A majority of Americans (76%) have an unfavorable view of China based on the four-point favorability question (Page 12)
- Conservative Republicans are 72% likely to have "very cold" feelings toward China, compared to 48% of moderate/liberal Republicans (Page 13)
- Men (51%) are more likely than women (43%) to have "very cold" feelings toward China (Page 13)
- A majority of those 50 and older (55%) have "very cold" opinions, while only 40% of those under 50 do (Page 13)
- 51% of those without a college degree feel "very cold" toward China, compared to 39% of college graduates (Page 13)
- An open-ended response from a 35-year-old woman cites human rights abuses and gender imbalances but also praises China's rich culture and inventions (Page 13)
- A majority of Americans (55%) describe China as a competitor, 34% as an enemy, and 9% as a partner (Page 14)
- 53% of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents view China as an enemy, compared to 20% of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents (Page 14)
- 64% of conservative Republicans view China as an enemy, while only 37% of moderate or liberal Republicans do (Page 14)
- 65% of Democrats and Democratic leaners describe the relationship as a competitor (Page 14)
- White adults (42%) are significantly more likely than Hispanic (21%) or Black adults (12%) to describe China as an enemy (Page 14)
- White Americans (6%) are less likely to describe China as a partner than Black (19%) or Hispanic (15%) Americans (Page 14)

VISUAL_EVIDENCE:
Tables:
- Table: Distribution of Feeling Thermometer Ratings for China (Page 10): Shows percentage of U.S. adults who rated China as "Very warm," "Somewhat warm," "Neutral," "Somewhat cold," or "Very cold" in 2018 and 2021, split by Total, Rep/Lean Rep, and Dem/Lean Dem.
- Table: Most Americans see China negatively (Page 13): Shows percentage of U.S. adults who rate China as "Very cold (0-24)" or "Somewhat cold (25-49)" on a feeling thermometer, broken down by demographic and political groups.
- Table: % who, on balance, think of China as a _ of the U.S. (Page 14): Displays distribution of responses across different demographic categories for three views: Partner, Competitor, and Enemy.

Figures:
- Chart: "Across modes and question types, Americans’ views of China have grown more negative in recent years" (Page 11): Line chart showing percentage of people with negative view of China from 2005 to 2021, comparing two survey methods: "Phone: four-point scale (% unfavorable)" and "ATP: feeling thermometer (% cold)".

Results indicated there were substantial differences by survey mode:  $66\%$  of those surveyed by phone had an unfavorable view of China, compared with  $79\%$  of those surveyed online. Because of these mode differences, we fielded two different survey questions on the ATP this year. The first is a "feeling thermometer," which asks people to evaluate their opinion of China on a 0 to 100 scale, where a rating of 51 or higher is "warm," 50 is neutral and below 50 is "cold." This question, which is the predominant focus of this report, was previously asked on the ATP in 2018 and 2016. Looking at these three points in time, we can see that the sharp increase in negative views of China that we have been documenting via our phone surveys is also evident via these online surveys. On this measure, those who say they are "cold" (0-49) toward China has increased from  $46\%$  in 2018 to  $67\%$  in 2021, or 21 percentage points. Second, we also asked our traditional four-point favorability question. Because of the mode differences previously identified, we decided that this number from the online survey was not directly comparable to the phone surveys previously conducted. But we want to "restart" this trend, beginning to measure it consistently on the ATP going forward, much as we have done so on the phone for the past 15 years. Results of this question indicate that a majority of Americans (76%) have an unfavorable view of China. This is consistent with the majority who say they are "cool" toward China on the feeling thermometer rating, though there are differences between the two measures due, in part, to the fact that the feeling thermometer has an explicit "neutral" category. (For more on how these two measures are similar and different, see "What different survey modes and question types can tell us about Americans' views of China.") Thanks to these two questions, we can see that unfavorable views of China increased dramatically since 2018, regardless of mode (phone vs. online) or measure (feeling thermometer or four-point scale).

This page from a Pew Research Center report presents findings on American public opinion regarding China, focusing on perceptions of China as an enemy and the prioritization of limiting its power and influence. The text highlights significant demographic differences, with older adults (49%) and those without college degrees (36%) more likely to view China as an enemy compared to younger adults (20%) and college graduates (30%). A key finding is that nearly half of Americans (48%) consider limiting China's power and influence a top foreign policy priority, up 16 percentage points since 2018. This sentiment is strongly partisan, with Republicans (63%) far more likely than Democrats (36%) to prioritize this goal. The data is visually supported by a line chart showing the increase in support across party lines and the total population from 2018 to 2021.

**Text Evidence:**
- 49% of adults aged 65 and older describe China as an enemy, compared to 20% of those under 30.
- 36% of those without a college degree see China as an enemy vs. 30% of college graduates.
- 48% of Americans think limiting China's power and influence should be a top priority, up 16 points from 2018.
- 63% of Republicans vs. 36% of Democrats prioritize limiting China's influence.
- For Republicans, it is the fifth most important issue; for Democrats, it ranks 12th.
- Other top priorities include protecting American jobs (75%), reducing infectious diseases (71%), and preventing WMD spread (64%).

**Visual Evidence:**
<chart_summary>Chart 1: "Both parties grow more supportive of curtailing China’s influence" - Line graph showing the percentage of U.S. adults who say limiting China's power and influence should be given top priority from 2018 to 2021. The red line (Rep/Lean Rep) shows a rise from 39% to 63%, the blue line (Dem/Lean Dem) from 26% to 36%, and the green line (Total) from 32% to 48%.</chart_summary>

This page from a Pew Research Center report presents findings on American public opinion regarding China, focusing on perceptions of China as an enemy and the prioritization of limiting its power and influence. The text highlights significant demographic differences, with older adults (49%) and those without college degrees (36%) more likely to view China as an enemy compared to younger adults (20%) and college graduates (30%). A key finding is that nearly half of Americans (48%) consider limiting China's power and influence a top foreign policy priority, up 16 percentage points since 2018. This sentiment is strongly partisan, with Republicans (63%) far more likely than Democrats (36%) to prioritize this goal. The data is visually supported by a line chart showing the increase in support across party lines and the total population from 2018 to 2021.

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- 53% of Americans are confident Biden can deal effectively with China (Page 18)
- This is the lowest level of confidence among six issues tested (Page 18)
- 67% have confidence in Biden to improve relationships with allies (Page 18)
- Around six-in-ten say they think he will be able to deal effectively with terrorism and global climate change (Page 18)

- Concerns about China's human rights policies have increased by 7 points since 2020 (Page 20)
- The U.S. trade deficit with China is seen as a very serious problem by about four-in-ten Americans (43%) (Page 20)

Americans anxious about China's technological and military power Americans express substantial concern when asked about eight specific issues in the U.S.- China relationship. About three-quarters or more say that each issue is at least somewhat serious. Still, four problems stand out for being ones that half or more describe as very serious: cyberattacks from China, the loss of U.S. jobs to China, China's growing military power and China's policies on human rights. Cyberattacks from China evoke the most concern: Roughly two-thirds consider digital attacks to be a very serious problem. This is a 7 percentage point increase from 2020. The share who see the loss of U.S. jobs to China as a very serious problem has increased by 6 points since 2020, to  $53\%$ . A similar share sees China's growing military power as a very serious problem (largely unchanged from the  $49\%$  who said the same last year). China's policies on human rights are seen as a very substantial problem for the U.S. by half of American adults, a 7-point increase since 2020. Results of previous telephone polls indicate that concerns about China's human rights policies increased between 2018 and 2020 as well. About four-in-ten Americans see the U.S. trade deficit with China – which decreased for the second year in a row – as a very serious problem, unchanged from 2020. Those with less than a college degree are more likely than those with a college degree or more education to see the trade deficit with China as a very serious problem. Similarly, those with lower levels of education are more likely to call the loss of U.S. jobs to China a very serious problem – but when it comes to other problems, people with different educational attainment levels largely agree.

This page from a Pew Research Center report presents findings from a February 2021 survey on American public opinion regarding China. The main content is divided into two sections: the first details negative perceptions of China's climate change policies, with 45% of Americans rating its job as "very bad." The second section focuses on human rights, showing that 90% of U.S. adults believe China does not respect personal freedoms, and 70% support prioritizing human rights promotion over economic relations. The page includes two bar charts illustrating these survey results.

**Text Evidence:**
- 45% of Americans say China has done a "very bad" job on climate change.
- Only 2% think China's approach to global warming has been "very good."
- 90% of U.S. adults say the Chinese government does not respect personal freedoms.

pages.ocr_text: Americans generally welcome international pupils, but widespread support for limits on Chinese students Although international student enrollment in the U.S. fell dramatically in 2020 because of COVID-19, during the 2019-2020 school year, more than 1 million international students studied at U.S. colleges and universities, comprising  $5.5\%$  of all student enrollment in American tertiary education. And generally speaking, the U.S. public sees these students in a positive light: Eight-in-ten Americans say it is good for U.S. colleges and universities to accept international students, while just  $19\%$  think the opposite. This sentiment is especially strong among certain subgroups in the U.S. population. Black and Hispanic Americans are more likely than White Americans to see international students as an asset. Likewise, younger people and those with a college degree say it is good for U.S. universities to accept international students. Partisanship also plays a role in views of international students. While at least two-thirds of supporters of each party see visiting students in a positive light,  $92\%$  of Democrats and Democrat-leaning independents hold this perspective, versus just  $67\%$  of Republicans and Republican leaners. Since 2009, the largest share of international students in the U.S. have come from China, according to the Institute of International Education. In 2019-2020, Chinese students comprised roughly a third of international students in American colleges and universities, and the number of Chinese students in U.S. academic institutions had nearly tripled over the previous decade. TOPICS: survey methodology, American Trends Panel (ATP), recruitment process, sample design, data collection protocol, weighting procedures, response rates, sampling error, data quality checks

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- The American Trends Panel (ATP) was created by Pew Research Center in 2014 and is managed by Ipsos (Page 35)
- Data is from a wave conducted Feb. 1 to Feb. 7, 2021, with 2,596 respondents out of 2,943 sampled, yielding an 88% response rate (Page 35)
- The cumulative response rate accounting for nonresponse and attrition is 4%, and the break-off rate is 2% (Page 35)
- The margin of sampling error for the full sample is plus or minus 2.7 percentage points (Page 35)
- Recruitment switched from telephone to address-based methods in August 2018 (Page 35)
- Three address-based recruitments were conducted in 2019 and 2020, inviting 17,161 adults and resulting in 15,134 joining (88%) (Page 36)
- 13,553 of the 25,076 individuals who ever joined remained active at the time of the survey (Page 36)
- The target population was non-institutionalized U.S. adults aged 18 and older (Page 36)
- The sample was allocated according to specific strata including tablet households, U.S.-born Hispanics, foreign-born Hispanics, high school education or less, foreign-born Asians, not registered to vote, people ages 18 to 34, uses internet weekly or less, non-Hispanic Black adults, nonvolunteers, and all other categories (Page 36)
- The questionnaire was developed by Pew Research Center in consultation with Ipsos and rigorously tested on PC and mobile devices (Page 36)
- Respondents received a post-paid incentive ranging from $5 to $20 (Page 36)
- Differential incentives were designed to increase participation among groups with low response propensities (Page 37)

Sample design The overall target population for this survey was non-institutionalized persons ages 18 and older, living in the U.S., including Alaska and Hawaii. Questionnaire development and testing The questionnaire was developed by Pew Research Center in consultation with Ipsos. The web program was rigorously tested on both PC and mobile devices by the Ipsos project management team and Pew Research Center researchers. The Ipsos project management team also populated test data which was analyzed in SPSS to ensure the logic and randomizations were working as intended before launching the survey. Incentives All respondents were offered a post-paid incentive for their participation. Respondents could choose to receive the post-paid incentive in the form of a check or a gift code to Amazon.com or could choose to decline the incentive. Incentive amounts ranged from  $5 to$ 20 depending on whether the respondent belongs to a part of the population that is harder or easier to reach.
